questions.stem: What is the difference between excretion and egestion?

options.text: They are the same process
Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products; egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces)
Egestion is the removal of metabolic waste; excretion is the removal of undigested food
Both involve the kidneys

questions.explanation: Excretion is the removal of waste products of metabolism (e.g., CO₂ from respiration, urea from deamination of amino acids). Egestion is the removal of undigested food from the body as faeces via the anus. Faeces were never absorbed into the body, so egestion is NOT excretion.

questions.stem: Where is urea produced, and from what process?

options.text: In the kidneys, from the breakdown of glucose
In the liver, from the deamination of excess amino acids
In the stomach, from protein digestion
In the lungs, from the breakdown of CO₂

questions.explanation: Urea is produced in the LIVER through deamination — the removal of the amino group (NH₂) from excess amino acids. The amino group is converted to ammonia, which is then converted to urea (less toxic). Urea is transported in the blood to the kidneys, where it is filtered out and excreted in urine.

questions.stem: What happens during ultrafiltration in the kidney?

options.text: Useful substances are reabsorbed from the nephron tubule back into the blood
Blood is filtered under high pressure in the glomerulus; small molecules pass into the Bowman's capsule while large proteins and blood cells remain in the blood
Urine is concentrated in the loop of Henle
Urea is broken down into ammonia

questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus (a knot of capillaries) inside Bowman's capsule. High blood pressure forces small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions, amino acids) through the capillary walls and basement membrane into the Bowman's capsule. Large molecules (proteins) and blood cells are too big to pass through and remain in the blood.

options.text: The filtration of blood in the glomerulus
The reabsorption of useful substances (glucose, amino acids, water, some ions) from the nephron tubule back into the blood
The secretion of hormones by the kidney
The production of urea in the liver

questions.explanation: Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule. Useful substances that were filtered out during ultrafiltration (all glucose, all amino acids, most water, and some ions) are reabsorbed back into the blood by active transport and osmosis. Urea and excess ions remain in the tubule and become part of the urine.

questions.stem: What is the effect of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) on the kidneys?

options.text: ADH decreases water reabsorption, producing dilute urine
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct, producing more concentrated urine
ADH breaks down urea into water
ADH increases the filtration rate in the glomerulus

questions.explanation: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) increases the permeability of the collecting duct walls, allowing more water to be reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis. This produces a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. More ADH is released when the body is dehydrated (blood water potential is low). Less ADH is released when well hydrated.

questions.stem: What is the role of the loop of Henle?

options.text: To filter blood under high pressure
To create a concentration gradient in the medulla, enabling water reabsorption from the collecting duct
To produce urea from amino acids
To store urine before it leaves the kidney

questions.explanation: The loop of Henle creates a high concentration of solutes (mainly sodium and chloride ions) in the medulla through a countercurrent multiplier system. This concentration gradient allows water to be reabsorbed from the collecting duct by osmosis when ADH is present, concentrating the urine.

questions.stem: Which part of the kidney contains the glomeruli and Bowman's capsules?

options.text: The medulla
The pelvis
The cortex
The ureter

questions.explanation: The glomeruli and Bowman's capsules are located in the cortex (outer region) of the kidney. The loops of Henle and collecting ducts extend into the medulla (inner region). The pelvis is the central cavity where urine collects before passing into the ureter.

questions.stem: What are the main functions of the liver?

options.text: Only to produce bile
Deamination of excess amino acids, detoxification of alcohol and drugs, bile production, and glycogen storage
Only to filter blood and produce urine
Only to store glucose as starch

questions.explanation: The liver has many functions including: deamination (breaking down excess amino acids, producing urea), detoxification (breaking down alcohol, drugs, and toxins), producing bile (for fat emulsification), storing glycogen (converted from glucose by insulin), and regulating blood glucose levels.

options.text: A surgical procedure to remove the kidneys
An artificial method of filtering the blood when the kidneys have failed, using a partially permeable membrane
A drug treatment that restores kidney function
A type of kidney transplant

questions.explanation: Dialysis is an artificial method of removing waste products (urea, excess ions) from the blood when the kidneys fail. In haemodialysis, blood passes over a partially permeable membrane with dialysis fluid on the other side. Small waste molecules diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, while useful substances (glucose) are retained. It must be done regularly (typically 3 times per week).

questions.stem: Where is the change in blood water potential detected for osmoregulation?

options.text: In the kidneys
In the hypothalamus of the brain
In the liver
In the adrenal glands

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus contains osmoreceptors that detect changes in blood water potential (concentration). When blood water potential drops (too little water/too many solutes), the hypothalamus stimulates the posterior pituitary gland to release more ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the kidneys.
